description: We are students from Chennai Institute of Technology taking on the MODIS & VIIRS Hot Spots challenge! We're building a Python app that merges fire detections from both NASA sensors into one fire calendar, and uses satellite orbits to show when a fire went unseen because no satellite was overhead. Looking for teammates skilled in data analysis, data visualization, Earth science, or video for our pitch!
summary: MOD-V SYNC is a sensor aware platform that brings into alignment active fire detections of NASA's MODIS and VIIRS satellites. MODIS satellite has been recording fires since 2000, while the VIIRS with higher resolution 375 m pixels detects around three to four times more fires. As the two satellites have differences in resolution, pass time and sensitivity, their detection records do not match each other and thus make long term fire analysis impossible. The pipeline based on NASA FIRMS data was created for analysis of fires in Chad (Sahel savanna) and Bolivia (Amazon edge) for 2018-2024 years. The pipeline performs cleaning and unification of both datasets, matching the detections of MODIS and VIIRS fires by distance and time using footprint based thresholds with clear labels of fire candidates, not confirmed fire events, finding fire hotspots using DBSCAN, comparing fire radiative power of individual sensors and testing the sensitivity of matching procedure to the selected distance threshold. The results were visualized using interactive dashboards including maps and charts.
details:
WHAT IT DOES:

MOD-V SYNC provides NASA’s two main fire detection databases in the same framework. There are often inconsistencies between the two datasets because the VIIRS instrument has a finer pixel size and can detect more fires than the MODIS, plus they pass by different times. The MOD-V SYNC portal makes these differences obvious rather than concealing them.

HOW IT WORKS:

1. Data: We utilize NASA FIRMS active-fire archives of MODIS (Collection 6.1) and VIIRS (375 m on NOAA-20) for two distinct study sites: Chad (Sahel savanna) and Bolivia (edge of Amazonia) for 2018 through 2024.

2. Cleaning: Validation and standardization of both datasets. Elimination of false detections, duplicates, and out-of-boundary points for each dataset and preservation of the original confidence level and Fire Radiative Power (FRP) values from each sensor.

3. Cross-sensor matching: Matching of each MODIS detection with the closest (in terms of the Haversine distance) VIIRS detection within the same day. Each match is considered a candidate if the distance does not exceed the threshold calculated based on the combined pixel footprint of both sensors. If a pair also has small temporal proximity, it is classified as spatiotemporal candidate. All other pairs of points are either ambiguous or unresolved. No candidate can be represented as confirmed same-fire event.

4. Hotspots: Cluster detection of hotspot areas using DBSCAN clustering method.

5. Analysis: Statistics for FRP values from both sensors, day vs. night distributions, time series of daily detections and sensitivity analysis (how matches count depends on the distance threshold)

6. Dashboard: The FastAPI backend handles all of the computations and feeds the results into an interactive Streamlit dashboard that has maps, charts, tables, quality reports, and CSV/JSON export capabilities.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT:

Scientists, forest management authorities, and air quality teams can learn where the sensors agree, disagree, and what causes it. The harmonized fire record will help provide fairer analysis of trends over time, especially as the aging MODIS satellites reach the end of their service, and VIIRS is taking the lead.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES:

Python 3.12, pandas, NumPy, PyArrow (Parquet), scikit-learn (BallTree, DBSCAN), FastAPI, Uvicorn, Streamlit, Plotly, Git, and GitHub. Data: NASA FIRMS.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE:

In contrast to a straightforward dataset merge, MOD-V SYNC treats the disagreement between sensors as a valuable source of information. Matching threshold for each detection is adjusted according to its true pixel size; every single match receives a proper status, and it can be easily verified in the dashboard...CONSIDERATIONS OF FACTORS

Honesty in science: no matches are referred to as confirmed fires, and no claims of accuracy are ever made without independent reference data.

Differences in sensors: confidence is numeric for MODIS and categorical for VIIRS, and therefore they are retained as is. FRP summing is never done with a pair of matches to prevent double counting.

Scale: roughly 4.6 million detections, processed with region and year filters, as well as matching on the same day.

Transparency: data quality measures, reproducibility and method documentation.
dataRefs: NASA FIRMS (MODIS and VIIRS active fire data)
